### Moment 1
What you did: "Mags, chum, I've lit every lamp in this town and not one of 'em throws a shadow where the sleepers lie. You had the peddler's wind-up toys on your cart before they went round the children. What did you pay for them, and what's left? Easy as winking, I'll find out what's in them."
Why: The peddler's toys are the one thing every sleeper has in common, and I bet Mags knows more about where they came from than she's letting on. I want to find the mechanism behind this before anyone else does, so the credit lands on me.
What happened: You step up to the tall-wheeled cart, the donkey eyeing your hat, and say your piece to the old woman in her shawls: every lamp in town lit, and still no shadow where the sleepers lie; the peddler's wind-up toys on her cart before they went round the children; what did she pay for them, and what's left?

Mags: She sucks her teeth, long and slow. "Never had a toy off that peddler, petal, nor wanted one. Nothing's free. Somebody's paying." She jerks her chin at the heap behind her. "Rags, bones, bottles an' bits, that's my cart, an' no tune wound up in any of it."

Mags: "Your lamps are lit, I'll give you that. But I've watched small shadows walk down Crooked Lane at night on their own. I keep my lantern burning an' I don't look." Duchess the donkey chews thoughtfully at the edge of a rag.

By the fountain, Marigold stands within earshot, the silver of a thimble catching the lamplight. Down the hill, something hums a lullaby and never quite finishes it. Mags is waiting to see what you make of that.
What you were told: Marigold Thimble says: "Goodness, Pip, you look like a rumpled pillowcase! Tell me about your brother's shadow: when did you last see it, and did he have one of those wind-up toys? And Mags, dear, you said small shadows walk down Crooked Lane at night. Would you point me which way they go?"
What happened: Marigold Thimble turned to Pip Pumbleton, teased her gently about looking like a rumpled pillowcase, and asked about her brother's shadow and the wind-up toys. Pip, gripping her cricket bat, said her brother Tod wound a tin rabbit the peddler gave him three days ago and fell asleep smiling, as did seven other children, and that at night their shadows get up off the walls and walk down Crooked Lane to a striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow. She said she had seen a big glass jar of grey stuff inside, and begged for someone to do something before midnight. Marigold also asked Mags which way the shadows walk, and Mags jerked her chin down Crooked Lane, toward the fog.

### Moment 2
What you were told: Marigold Thimble says: "Goodness, Pip, yes, I'll help, and you'll not do it alone with a cricket bat and no sleep. Come on, down Crooked Lane to the striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow, and we'll keep to the shadows' own path. Dilly, dear, will you light our way with that pole? Nobody's lamps are doing better work tonight."
What happened: Marigold answered Pip's plea aloud, said she would help, and called Dilly to come and light the way with the lamplighter's pole. Then she tucked her shawl tight and went out of the square by the south road, down Crooked Lane.
What happened: Hobb came down out of the Tock Tower into the square, looked about the houses as if seeking a hearth, and stood a moment by the south road.
What you did: I grab my lamplighter's pole, give Pip a wink and a pat on the shoulder, and say, "Easy as winking, chum. Marigold's not going down Crooked Lane alone, and neither are we. Hobb, you lead the way with your lantern, and I'll keep the pole high so nothing sneaks past us in the fog."
Why: I want the credit for cracking this before anyone else, so I'm joining Marigold's party now, lighting their path and keeping an eye on the shadows. If the striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow holds whatever is stealing the children's shadows, I'll be the one who put a stop to it.
What happened: You grab your lamplighter's pole, give Pip a wink and a pat on the shoulder, and tell the square it's easy as winking: Marigold isn't going down Crooked Lane alone, and neither are you. You tell Hobb to lead the way and say you'll keep the pole high so nothing sneaks past in the fog. Then you go out by the south road.

The lane wiggles downhill between garden walls, with lamplight, dark, lamplight again. Marigold Thimble stands here, and Hester Gimbal beside her with a notebook and a little iron poker. A round grating in the gutter makes a soft wet sound, as if someone were patiently licking their lips.

Small shadows slip past your boots, child-sized, trotting downhill with nobody to cast them. Below, the lane spills out into Gloomer's Meadow, where a striped glow waits in the fog and a lullaby hums, never quite finishing its tune.
What changed: you went from The Lopsided Square to Crooked Lane.
What happened: Somewhere close, a soft sing-song voice is calling "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" and a tray of tin things hums along.

### Moment 3
What you did: "Hold up, chum. That grating's been licking its lips at us, so before we go on, I'm going to give it a poke with my pole to see what answers. Hester, keep that little poker ready. Marigold, you walk point with me, and we'll follow the shadows south together, lamplight all the way."
Why: I want to see what's under that grating before anyone else does, since it might be where the shadows or the toys are coming from. If I find the source of this trouble in Crooked Lane, the credit will be mine.
What happened: "Hold up, chum," you say, and the lane stops with you, halfway down the hill, where the lamps are spaced too far apart. Marigold and Hester are beside you, Hester with her iron poker in hand. "That grating's been licking its lips at us, so I'm going to give it a poke with my pole. Marigold, you walk point with me, and we'll follow the shadows south together, lamplight all the way."

You lean out and set the end of the lamplighter's pole against the round iron grating, with its holes shaped like little smiles. The soft wet licking underneath pauses. Then a whisper rises through the holes, patient and sing-song:

The grating: "Down in the dark where the drippings drain, who will answer me, once again?"

Nothing else comes up. The licking starts again, slow and content. Past your boots, a small child-sized shadow with nobody to cast it slips by and trots on downhill toward the meadow, where a faint striped glow drifts up through the fog.

The lane runs on south into the dark, and the others are waiting on your step.
What you were told: Marigold Thimble says: "Goodness, that voice is like wet flannel. Let's leave it to its licking and not answer it, whatever it rhymes. Follow the shadows south, quiet as pins, and keep that lamp low when we reach the meadow."
What happened: Marigold kept well clear of the drain-grating, tucked her shawl in tight, and whispered that they should leave the voice to its licking and follow the shadows south as quiet as pins. Then she took the lead and went off down Crooked Lane toward the striped glow in the fog, out of sight of the others.
What you were told: Hester Gimbal says: "Fascinating, she's gone on without us! Dilly, my dear colleague, quick, bring that lamp, and keep an ear out for that toy-seller crooning about."
What happened: Hester called after Marigold that she had gone on without them, urged Dilly to bring the lamp and listen for the toy-seller crooning about, and then hurried south down Crooked Lane with her iron poker up and her notebook under her arm, following the trail of trotting shadows into Gloomer's Meadow, where she joined Marigold by the striped wagon.

### Moment 4
What you did: I stop at the top of Crooked Lane, alone now, and call down toward the meadow: "Marigold! Hester! Wait for Dilly, chum, I'm coming with the pole!" Then I start after them, keeping the lamp high.
Why: The others have gone on without me, and I won't let Marigold and Hester get the credit for the striped wagon. I'm working toward finding the glass jar and the shadow-stealer before the Thirteenth Stroke, so that the whole town knows whose lamp showed the way.
What happened: At the top of Crooked Lane you stop, alone, and call down toward the meadow: "Marigold! Hester! Wait for Dilly, chum, I'm coming with the pole!" Then you start after them, keeping the lamp high, and the lane wiggles you down from light to dark to light, past small shadows trotting the same way without a look back.

The lane spills out into Gloomer's Meadow. Long grey grass, fog to the knee, and a ring of mushrooms leaning in to listen. In the middle stands the tall striped wagon with its crooked chimney and its keyhole door, a lantern swaying above it and a lullaby humming from inside. A patient line of small shadows waits at the foot of the steps.

Marigold is crouched in the grass with her shawl drawn dark around her. Hester is a tall shape bent to the gap of the wagon door. The steps are empty of any peddler, and the door stands a little open.
What changed: you went from Crooked Lane to Gloomer's Meadow.

### Moment 5
What you were told: Marigold Thimble says: "Goodness, Hester, what do you see? Is the jar in there, and is the peddler home?" Hush, Dilly, keep the lamp shaded and quiet. We'll wait here at the steps for Hester's word before any of us goes in."
What happened: Marigold crept through the grass to Hester's side and whispered, asking what she saw, whether the jar was in the wagon and whether the peddler was home. She waved Dilly down low and hissed for the lamp to be kept shaded and quiet, then waited at the wagon steps for Hester's word before anyone went in.
What you did: I stand at the wagon steps, keep my lamp shaded, and whisper to Marigold and Hester, "Easy as winking, chum, but nobody goes through that door until we know what's inside. Hester, tell us what you see. I'll hold the pole steady and watch the shadows in case they try to slip past us."
Why: Marigold and Hester are the only ones close enough to see inside the wagon, and I'd rather get the first real look than rush through the door and spoil it for everyone. If the glass jar and the peddler are in there, I want to be the one who knew where to watch before they got away.
What happened: You stand at the foot of the wagon steps with your lamp shaded, the lamplighter's pole planted steady beside you. The fog lies cold around your knees, and the lantern over the keyhole door makes a small gold smear in the grey.

Dilly: "Easy as winking, chum, but nobody goes through that door until we know what's inside. Hester, tell us what you see. I'll hold the pole steady and watch the shadows in case they try to slip past us."

Marigold and Hester are close beside you. The line of small shadows waits in its patient file at the steps, and the lullaby keeps drifting out through the keyhole door.
What you were told: Hester Gimbal says: "My dear colleagues, no peddler, but there's a glass jar on the table full of grey stuff that turns as if it's breathing, and the shadows go in through the keyhole one by one. Hypothesis: that jar is where the sleep is kept, or the shadows, or both! Test: Dilly, keep the pole across the door so no more go in; Marigold, keep watch on the meadow; and we three go in together and have a proper look at that jar before he comes back."
What happened: Hester leaned back from the open wagon door and whispered fast to Marigold and Dilly. She told them the peddler was not inside, but a glass jar of grey stuff stood on a table, turning as if it breathed, and the shadows went in by the keyhole one at a time. She proposed that Dilly hold the pole across the door, that Marigold watch the meadow, and that all three go in together for a proper look at the jar before the peddler came back.
